name: Amsi
title: Priest in the lineage of Immer, mentioned in the book of Nehemiah and First Chronicles
lifespan: Uncertain, probably around the 5th century BC or earlier
summary: Amzi was a priest mentioned in the genealogy in the book of Nehemiah (Neh 11:13), and probably also in 1 Chronicles (1 Chr 9:12), where the name form Meshillemith/Meshullamot may cover an overlapping family member. He belonged to the priestly family of Immer, one of the most prominent priestly lines in Israel, and was a link in the priestly lineage between his father Zechariah and the other ancestors tracing back to Immer. This priestly heritage was passed on to those who served in the temple in Jerusalem after returning from the Babylonian exile. The inclusion of Amzi in the genealogy testifies to the great emphasis placed on preserving the priestly lines, which was essential for ensuring legitimate temple service in the rebuilt sanctuary.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in the genealogy in the book of Nehemiah
keyEvents.description: Amsi is listed in the genealogy of priests who lived in Jerusalem after the return from Babylon. He is mentioned as the son of Zechariah in the priestly lineage that traces back to Immer.

keyEvents.title: Parallel lineage in First Chronicles
keyEvents.description: In First Chronicles there is a parallel list of priests in Jerusalem, where the name forms vary somewhat from those in the book of Nehemiah. Amsi's ancestral line can be recognized in the list leading back to Immer.

versions.summary: Amsi was a Levitical priest mentioned in the genealogy in the book of Nehemiah. He was a descendant of Aaron's sons and served in the temple after the return from exile in Babylon. His role was to maintain the priestly service in the rebuilt temple in Jerusalem.
versions.title: Levitical priest in the time of Nehemiah
versions.reason: [major] According to Neh 11:12-13, the genealogy is: ...Amsi, son of Zechariah, son of Pashhur, son of Malkijah. But in the parallel text in 1 Chr 9:12, the order is slightly different. Zechariah as father of Amsi seems reasonable based on Neh 11:12-13, but the id 'zechariah-priest' should be verified against the actual id used in the database.; [major] According to Neh 11:12-13, Amsi is the son of Zechariah, and Pelaliah (or Pelajah) is not mentioned as a son of Amsi in this genealogy. The genealogy in Neh 11:12-13 goes: Adaiah, son of Jeroham, son of Pelaliah, son of Amsi. Thus, Pelaliah is the son of Amsi, not a child in the modern sense, but an intermediate link in the lineage. The reference appears correct, but it should be verified that 'pelaliah' is the proper id.; [minor] The summary states that Amsi was "a descendant of Aaron's sons," but more precisely he belonged to the priestly family of Immer (via the Pashhur/Malkijah line). This could be improved with more precise wording.; [minor] The second key event entry ("Part of the priesthood in Jerusalem") is somewhat speculative. The text in Neh 11:10-14 lists priests who lived in Jerusalem, but does not explicitly state that Amsi himself served—he is mentioned as an ancestor in the genealogy. Amsi may have lived generations earlier.; [major] The key event "Restoration of spiritual life" with references to Neh 12:1-2 and Neh 10:28-29 does not concern Amsi. Neh 12:1-2 lists priests who returned with Zerubbabel, and Neh 10:28-29 deals with the people's renewal of the covenant. Amsi is not mentioned in either passage, and the connection is too speculative.; [minor] The lifespan "c. 450 BC" is uncertain. Amsi is mentioned as a link in a genealogy, and it is not certain that he lived as late as 450 BC. He may have lived earlier, depending on how many generations the lineage spans. A broader dating might be more appropriate.; [minor] The reference to 1 Chr 9:12 (bookId 13) for the genealogy from Immer is relevant and correct. In this text, Amasai (which may correspond to Amsi) is mentioned in the genealogy via Pashhur, son of Malkijah. Good parallel reference.; [minor] The title "Levitical priest in Nehemiah's time" may be imprecise. Amsi is an intermediate link in a genealogy and may not have lived during Nehemiah's own lifetime. A more neutral title such as "Priest mentioned in the genealogical register of the book of Nehemiah" might fit better.

versions.summary:
Amzi was a priest mentioned in the genealogies in the book of Nehemiah and 1 Chronicles.  
He belonged to the priestly family of Immer and was part of the lineage that included Zechariah (his father) and Pelaliah (his son).  
Through this line, the priestly inheritance was passed on to those who served in the temple in Jerusalem after returning from the Babylonian exile.  
Amzi's place in the genealogy testifies to the importance of preserving the priestly lines to ensure legitimate temple service.

versions.title: Priest in the lineage of Immer, mentioned in the book of Nehemiah
versions.reason: [major] In Neh 11:13 the lineage is: Amasai (Amsi) son of Zechariah, son of Pashhur, son of Malkijah – but 'zechariah-priest' as an ID for the father may be imprecise. More importantly: in the text itself, Zechariah is the father of Amsi, but it should be verified that the ID 'zechariah-priest' actually refers to the correct Zechariah in the system. Leave this as is if the ID mapping is correct.; [major] According to Neh 11:13, the lineage stating Masillai/Pelaljah son of Amsi is incorrect. The order in Neh 11:13 is: '...Amasai, son of Zechariah, son of Pashhur, son of Malkijah'. Thus, Amsi is the son of Zechariah. But who is Amsi's son? In Neh 11:13 going upward: 'Amasjai son of Asarel, son of Akzai, son of Meshullamoth, son of Immer' — this is a different line. Pelaljah is mentioned in Neh 11:12 as part of another lineage. The lineage in Neh 11:13: Masillai/Amasjai - Asarel - Akzai - Meshullamoth - Immer. Amsi's place is different. In 1 Chr 9:12: 'Adaiah son of Jeroham, son of Pashhur, son of Malkijah, and Maasai son of Adiel, son of Jahzerah, son of Meshullam, son of Meshillemith, son of Immer'. Pelaljah does not appear to be Amsi's son in these texts. Neh 11:12 contains a different lineage (the Seraiah line) where Pelaljah occurs. The child relationship 'pelalja' should be removed or corrected.; [minor] The summary states that Pelaljah was Amsi's son, but this is doubtful based on the biblical text. Neh 11:12-13 contains two separate lineages: verse 12 concerns the Seraiah line (where Pelaljah is mentioned), and verse 13 concerns the Amasjai line (where Amsi/Zechariah is mentioned). The summary should be corrected so that it does not claim Pelaljah was Amsi's son.; [minor] The title is fine, but could be refined to mention that he also appears in First Chronicles, reflecting both sources.; [minor] Verse 12 is included, but Amsi is specifically mentioned in verse 13 (Neh 11:13). Verse 12 belongs to a different lineage (the Seraiah line). It is more precise to refer only to verse 13.

footnotes.text: The name Amsi (Hebrew: אַמְצִי, 'Amtsi') probably means 'my strength' or 'strong', derived from the root א-מ-ץ which means 'to be strong'. This is a rare name in the Old Testament and occurs only in priestly genealogies.

The priestly family of Immer was one of the prominent priestly families that returned from exile in Babylon. The family of Immer is mentioned among those who were assigned service shifts in the temple already during David's time (1 Chron 24:14), as the sixteenth of twenty-four service divisions.

The genealogies in Nehemiah 11 and 1 Chronicles 9 share many parallels but also differ in name forms and order. This may be because they represent different stages of the same tradition, or that the name forms evolved over time through copying. In 1 Chronicles 9:12, a name form is used that is likely a variant of Amsi.

After returning from the Babylonian exile, it was crucial to document the genealogies of the priests to ensure that only legitimate priests served in the temple. Ezra 2:62–63 tells of priests who were excluded from service because they could not prove their lineage.

In rabbinic tradition, the genealogies of the priests were carefully preserved, and there were special archives in the temple where family records were kept. This practice reflected the belief that priestly legitimacy was tied to descent from Aaron through documented lineages.

Nehemiah 11:12–13 contains two parallel genealogies for priests living in Jerusalem: the Seraiah line (verse 12) and the Amashai line (verse 13). Amsi belongs to the latter, which traces back to Immer. These two lines represent different priestly families with different responsibilities in the temple.
